latin.659: SED pergamus. Ex versu sequente, quo Apostolus id quod dixerat, peccatum introiisse in mundum & omnes homines peccasse, probat, tu nescio quid argumenti colligis, quod & praecedente illo tuo a me iam refutato ac absurdis obruto nititur, & a te ipso continuo destruitur.
latin.660: Nam, inquit Apostolus, Usque ad legem peccatum erat in mundo. Peccatum vero non imputatur, quum nulla lex est. Sic, inquis, ex hoc dicto Apostoli argumentor. Peccatum illud, de quo loquitur Apostolus versu immediate praecedenti, est peccatum illud quod fuit in mundo usque ad legem, ut patet ex sequela & textura verborum, maxime ex illa particula γάρ, quae est rationalis. Hoc concedo, & ut memineris rogo, nam & verum est, & ad tuam sententiam evertendam, meam autem firmandam apprime utile.
latin.661: Subsumis, sed peccatum primum Adami fuit illud peccatum de quo locutus est Apostolus versu immediate praecedenti, ut supra probavimus.
latin.662: Nititur igitur haec tua propositio superiori tua argumentatione, quam vides a nobis capite praecedente multis telis confossam ac confectam, ut iure meo possim eius loco hanc ponere, Atqui vitium originale omnibus hominibus inhaerens est illud peccatum de quo loquutus est Apostolus versu immediate praecedenti, ut supra probavi. Ergo peccatum illud quod fuit in mundo usque ad legem est vitium originale omnibus inhaerens, quod vitium omnibus, nisi condonetur per Christum, imputari non fateor modo, sed contendo etiam.
latin.663: Verum ego alia ratione hoc idem argumentum in te torquebo, quae non nitetur superiori disputatione, sed eam suo proprio pondere augeat, eoque gravi & momentoso. Peccatum illud, de quo loquitur Apostolus versu immediate praecedente, est peccatum illud quod fuit in mundo usque ad legem, ut recte probasti. Atqui peccatum primum actuale Adami non est peccatum illud quod fuit in mundo usque ad legem. Ergo peccatum primum actuale Adami non est peccatum illud de quo loquitur Apostolus versu immediate praecedenti, ac proinde non est peccatum illud quod in mundum, id est, te interprete in nos, introiit, & quo omnes homines peccaverunt.
latin.664: Maiorem propositionem negare non potes; est enim tua, & si negares, facile, ut tu recte observasti, ex particula causali γάρ, & textura disputationis Apostolicae revinci posses. Minor suapte luce manifesta est. Nonne enim perspicuum est peccatum primum actuale, quod actio fuit singularis & numero una, vix horam unam durans, non fuisse in mundo toto illo tempore quod ab eo perpetrato ad legem usque Mosis fluxit, hoc est, non perdurasse in mundo spatio duorum millium & quingentorum annorum? Hoc certe convenit vitio originali, quod tamdiu est in mundo quamdiu est genus humanum: sed non convenit uni actioni individuae & singulari, quae dum fit praeterit cum tempore, & ut non desiit esse in mundo vivente Adamo cuius accidens quoddam fuit, nimirum actio, tamen eo extincto qui potuit eadem numero in mundo, id est in hominibus, esse bis mille & quingentos annos? Noli confugere ad imputationem quam iam saepius confutavi: nam aliud est peccatum esse in mundo, aliud imputari mundo: hoc ordine naturae sequitur, illud praecedit. Adde quod negare non potes, certe non debes, revera toto illo tempore peccatum in mundo seu hominibus fuisse, immo regnasse obedientibus eius concupiscentiis hominibus.

pass_a.659: Placeus opens Cap. X: from the next verse, where Paul proves that sin entered the world and all sinned, you gather some argument that rests on your prior case—already refuted and buried in absurdities—and that you yourself promptly destroy.
pass_a.660: Paul: until the law sin was in the world; sin is not imputed when there is no law. You argue: the sin of the prior verse is that pre-law world-sin, clear from the verbal texture and especially γάρ. Placeus grants that major and asks you to remember it—it is true and useful to overturn your view and firm his.
pass_a.661: Next you fold in the minor: Adam first-sin equals the sin named in the verse just before, the point you say was already proved above.
pass_a.662: So your proposition hangs on that prior argumentation, which Cap. IX already riddled with many shafts. Placeus may lawfully swap in: inherent original vice in all is the sin of the prior verse. Therefore the pre-law world-sin is that inherent original vice—which he not only admits but contends is imputed to all unless forgiven through Christ.
pass_a.663: He turns the same argument another way, on its own weight. Major (yours): the prior-verse sin is the pre-law world-sin. Minor: Adam’s first actual sin is not that enduring world-sin. Conclusion: Adam’s first actual sin is not the sin that entered the world—into us, on your reading—and by which all sinned.
pass_a.664: You cannot deny the major—it is yours, and the causal particle plus the apostolic texture would convict a denial. The minor is self-evident: a singular one-hour act did not last the roughly twenty-five hundred years from its commission to Moses; that span fits original vice coextensive with the human race, not one individual action that passes as it is done. Even if that act remained in the world during Adam life as his accident, once he was dead the same numerical act could not still be in men for those millennia. Do not flee to the imputation already often refuted: being in the world is one thing, being imputed to the world another—the latter follows, the former precedes. And you must grant that through all that time sin really was in the world or in men, and even reigned as men obeyed its lusts.

659: From the following verse, by which the Apostle proves what he had said—that sin entered into the world and all men sinned—you gather I know not what argument, which both rests on that prior case of yours already refuted by me and overwhelmed with absurdities, and is continually destroyed by you yourself.
660: For, says the Apostle, Until the law sin was in the world. But sin is not imputed when there is no law.
Thus, you say, I argue from this saying of the Apostle.

That sin of which the Apostle speaks in the immediately preceding verse is that sin which was in the world until the law, as is plain from the sequel and texture of the words, especially from that particle γάρ, which is causal.
This I concede, and I ask that you remember it, for it is true, and highly useful for overturning your opinion and establishing mine.
661: You subsume: but the first sin of Adam was that sin of which the Apostle spoke in the immediately preceding verse, as we proved above.
662: Therefore this proposition of yours rests on your prior argumentation, which you see riddled and finished by us in the preceding chapter with many shafts, so that by my right I may put this in its place: But original vice inherent in all men is that sin of which the Apostle spoke in the immediately preceding verse, as I proved above.
Therefore that sin which was in the world until the law is original vice inherent in all, which vice I not only confess but even contend is to be imputed to all, unless it is forgiven through Christ.
663: But I will turn this same argument against you by another reason, which will not lean on the prior dispute, but will strengthen it by its own weight, and that a heavy and momentous one.
That sin of which the Apostle speaks in the immediately preceding verse is that sin which was in the world until the law, as you rightly proved.
But the first actual sin of Adam is not that sin which was in the world until the law.

Therefore the first actual sin of Adam is not that sin of which the Apostle speaks in the immediately preceding verse, and so is not that sin which entered into the world—that is, on your interpretation, into us—and by which all men sinned.
664: You cannot deny the major proposition; for it is yours, and if you denied it you could easily, as you yourself rightly observed, be convicted from the causal particle γάρ and the texture of the apostolic disputation.
The minor is clear by its own light.

Is it not plain that the first actual sin, which was a singular action and one in number, lasting scarcely one hour, was not in the world through all that time which flowed from its commission until the law of Moses—that is, that it did not endure in the world for the space of two thousand five hundred years?

This certainly fits original vice, which is in the world as long as the human race is; but it does not fit one individual and singular action, which as it is done passes with time, and though it did not cease to be in the world during Adam’s life—whose accident it was, namely an action—yet once he was dead, who could that same numerical act be in the world, that is in men, for two thousand five hundred years?

Do not flee to the imputation which I have already often refuted: for it is one thing for sin to be in the world, another for it to be imputed to the world; the latter follows in the order of nature, the former precedes.
Add that you cannot deny—certainly you ought not—that through all that time sin really was in the world or in men, and even reigned as men obeyed its lusts.
